title: Critical Thinking, Expertise and Intelligence
author: Peter Ellerton
summary: Peter Ellerton distinguishes three often-conflated concepts: intelligence (general cognitive capacity), expertise (high-level domain performance through deliberate practice), and critical thinking (learnable disciplinary reasoning norms). Critical thinking is the most actionable in education—students can be taught to recognize valid inferences, evaluate evidence, and question assumptions. Expertise develops through deliberate practice paired with critical reflection on one's own performance. Teaching critical thinking explicitly—identifying reasoning patterns, standards of argument, and conceptual distinctions—transforms how students approach learning across disciplines. Critical thinking acts as a driver of expertise development, making it essential for educators to stop treating thinking ability as fixed intelligence.
points: Intelligence contains almost no content knowledge and remains largely unactionable for teachers, while critical thinking consists of identifiable reasoning practices that can be taught explicitly.
Critical thinking is a discipline, not a trait—students can learn how good arguments work, how evidence supports claims, and how assumptions operate within reasoning.

Expertise develops primarily through deliberate practice (performance, reflection, adjustment of mental models), not through intelligence, and critical thinking significantly improves this reflective process.
When education focuses too heavily on intelligence, it risks treating thinking as fixed; when it focuses on critical thinking, it recognizes good reasoning as something people can learn and improve.

All disciplines have critical thinking embedded in their methodology, but most remain implicit in teaching rather than explicit, leaving students expected to think critically without understanding what that actually involves.
quotes: Intelligence is usually treated as a general cognitive capacity. People often think of it as something you're born with: the mental horsepower that allows you to process information quickly, recognise patterns or make connections.
Critical thinking is not a trait. It is a discipline of thinking that can be taught, practised and improved.

One of the most powerful aspects of critical thinking is the attention it gives to inferences. Knowledge matters, but the most important cognitive work we do with knowledge is often drawing conclusions from it, including when we infer to new knowledge claims.

Expertise does not automatically produce critical thinking. Being highly skilled in a domain does not guarantee that someone reasons well about broader issues. But critical thinking can significantly improve the process of developing expertise.

When education focuses too heavily on intelligence, it risks treating thinking ability as fixed. When it focuses on critical thinking, it recognises that good reasoning is something people can learn to do better.” Archived from Critical Thinking Explained on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
